newsitem.title: IRAN: FEATURE - Tehran dwellers seek release from big city.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tehran dwellers seek release from big city.

text.p: The Iranian couple grasped each other, kissed and laughed amongst friends on the steep rocky footpaths of Tehran's mountains, displays of affection that would not be tolerated on the city's busy streets below.

Down the pathway a man in his early twenties leaned on a tattered umbrella and sang Persian verse to his audience of snow-capped mountain tops and waterfalls while a friend hawked local pistachios and dried dates to passing walkers.

Tehran's mountain tracks have a romantic tinge but their real importance to some of the Iranian capital's seven million people are as a release from the city's traffic, smog, high prices and the strict Islamic codes that saturate daily life.
"No money, no jobs there...The air is better here," said a middle-aged woman, pointing down the mountainside to bustling central Tehran, just a 15-minute drive away.

It is at the Darekeh mountain range, the growing number of Tehran's public parks and in private homes where a glimpse of how less-traditionalist Iranians seek a break from one of the world's most densely-populated and rigorous cities.
This is the slice of life between the revolutionary state slogans and images that have become synonymous with Iran.
Eighteen years after the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini overthrew the secular monarchy of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, Iran still displays revolutionary zeal.

The Islamic Republic's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei drew tens of thousands of supporters at a Friday prayer meeting this month at Tehran university and called for death to what the country calls its enemies -- the United States and Israel.
Public morality, behaviour and dress, particularly for women, is strictly monitored by a host of security agencies.
Courts have been set up to fight Western cultural influences and the law severely restricts contacts between unmarried people of different sexes who are not related.
Political candidates must pass a revolutionary litmus test if they are allowed to run for office and satellite television is officially banned though discreetly still exists.

In the relaxed atmosphere of Tehran's mountains and public parks, the state still has a presence with painted portraits of its leaders expounding Islamic and revolutionary principles lining the early paved stages of the hill climb.

Women climbers still have to cover themselves but some reveal more of their face under colourful headscarves and let a modest fringe fall onto their foreheads, freedoms that could incur wrath down in Tehran.

Chitgar Park, five kilometres (three miles) from the capital's western suburbs, is a pleasing wooded parkland dotted with winding cycle paths, easy walking routes and picnic tables for Tehran's increasing urban and young population.
The authorities are planning to develop Chitgar as a Disneyland-style park but the 30-foot (nine metre) high poster at the cycle park's entrance dispels any notion of California escapism.
"The future belongs to the Hezbollah" reads a billboard filled with the faces of Khomeini and Khamenei.
In a reference to the headdress and other garments women must wear to conceal themselves, a second adjoining poster carries the message "Hejab is dignity not restriction."
Women and men are not allowed to cycle together at Chitgar after protests by local conservative militia last year resulted in separate cycle tracks being enforced.
This does not stop people coming on a cold winter afternoon and paying the equivalent of $1.65 for entrance.

"We come here once a month in the winter and twice in the summer...It is not expensive," said a father who had driven his wife and two young children to the park in their rapidly ageing and battered Paykan car, Tehran's most popular model.
For Tehran's young, the mountains and parks are the few places where they can meet the opposite sex with a reduced risk of being questioned by the police.
On the mountainside young men, one dressed in a sweatshirt emblazoned with the name of America's Chicago Bulls basketball team, looked out for potential new female friends.
"There is no proper way for our young people to meet. Finding somewhere is a problem," said an Iranian mother.
Her son had recently been taken to a police station after he was stopped talking with his girlfriend outside a Tehran cinema.
But for those playing volleyball and soccer on the broad concrete walkways of the Laleh park in central Tehran, the revolution is secondary. This is a day of rest.
